paras: The lynching of W. H. Handley took place on the night of July 31, 1888, when a mob of about fifty armed men broke into the jail at Carthage, Smith County, Tennessee, took out Handley, and hanged him to a tree. Handley, about 23, was awaiting trial, set for the next day, on a charge of killing a deputy sheriff the previous September. The papers noted the resistance of the sheriff and his posse, who exchanged about thirty shots with the mob before it reached the prisoner.

Deputy Sheriff J. B. Warman was killed on September 17, 1887, about a mile and a half from Rome, Smith County, while returning from the fair with a prisoner named Adams. According to the Memphis Appeal, Handley overtook the deputy, demanded Adams' release, and shot him when he refused; a Nashville dispatch likewise said Handley killed Warman "while trying to rescue a prisoner." Arrested soon afterward near Riddleton, Handley denied any connection with the killing.

The Appeal reported that officers had to evade three mobs after the arrest, hiding Handley in the woods before moving him by way of New Middleton and Lebanon to the Nashville jail, where he was held for his protection. He was brought back to Carthage only a few days before the date set for his trial.

The mob reached the Carthage jail at 10 o'clock according to the wire report, or 11 o'clock according to a Carthage special, and found it guarded by the sheriff and a posse. The sheriff pleaded with the men to let the law take its course and refused to give up the keys, saying he would die before surrendering them. The mob then broke down the barred door to the jailer's quarters and battered its way into Handley's cell with axes and crowbars.

With a rope around his neck, Handley was hurried across the river and hanged to a large tree within sight of the jail. About thirty shots were exchanged between the mob and the posse, but no one was reported hurt. When the body was brought into Carthage the next morning it showed severe bruises and two large cuts on the head, believed to have been made with a gun butt.

Coroner A. M. Fisher held an inquest that morning, and the jury returned a verdict of death by hanging "at the hands of unknown parties." Handley's mother and family, arriving for the trial, learned of his death on reaching town, and his mother was reported prostrated. The Appeal described great excitement in the area, with public opinion "about qualily [equally] divided for and against Handley." No report of arrests or of a grand jury inquiry appears in the coverage.

The Memphis Appeal gave the fullest account under the headline "MOB LAW," with decks praising "The Courageous Sheriff" and describing "The Self-Assumed Court and Jury" overpowering him. The same report called Handley "The Murderer of Deputy Sheriff Warman" even as it noted his denial and the wounds on his body. The Atlanta Constitution ran the first half of the same Carthage special on August 7 under the headline "He Escaped Three Mobs."

A shorter Carthage wire, which made no mention of shooting, appeared on August 1 and 2 in the Washington Evening Star, the Springfield Daily Republic, the Johnson City Comet and the Salt Lake Herald, under headings such as "Lynch Law" and "Lynched." It referred to Handley as "the murderer" and spelled his name variously as Handly and Hannaly, while the Lebanon Express in Oregon carried it as late as August 10 with the name "O. H. Handly."

Weekly news digests reduced the event to a single line, the San Antonio Daily Light adding that the sheriff "made a heroic defense against the mob, but to no purpose." In Tennessee, the Pulaski Citizen noted only that Handley had been taken out "one night last week and hanged."

bases: Fifty armed men broke into the Carthage jail, took out W. H. Handley, held for trial on a murder charge, and hanged him to a tree (A1, A2, A4).

A mob of fifty armed men took Handley from the jail against the sheriff's resistance and hanged him the night before his trial for killing a deputy sheriff (A1, A4, A5); the Memphis Appeal called the mob a 'Self-Assumed Court and Jury' (A4).
The Carthage wire (A1, A2), a separate Carthage special (A4, A16), a Nashville dispatch (A5) and a Tennessee local note (A23) agree that a mob took Handley from the Carthage jail and hanged him.

framing.detail: The Memphis Appeal headlined 'MOB LAW' and the 'Courageous Sheriff', mocked the 'Self-Assumed Court and Jury', yet called Handley 'the Murderer of Deputy Sheriff Warman' and detailed the wounds on his body.
Northern and western papers ran the brief Carthage wire under 'Lynch Law' or 'Lynched', calling Handley 'the murderer' who 'killed' the deputy.
The Atlanta Constitution headed the Carthage special 'He Escaped Three Mobs'.
Weekly news digests reduced the event to one line, the San Antonio Daily Light adding that the sheriff 'made a heroic defense'.
